message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What You’re Generally Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|-----------------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.).
• Must comply with all applicable building, health, and safety codes. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent, repair & deduct, or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” claim in small‑claims court. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if expressly stated in the lease and are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re experiencing hardship. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to quiet enjoyment of the premises. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry to the landlord or local authorities. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord may terminate early only for cause (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal Fair Housing laws. Discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes is illegal. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the statutory eviction procedure (notice, filing, court order).
• Eviction cannot be carried out without a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly; consider seeking legal counsel or mediation. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for:
– Unpaid rent
– Damage beyond normal wear & tear
– Cleaning costs if the unit was left dirty
– Replacement of lost keys or locks
– Other costs specified in the lease | • Review the lease for any specific deduction clauses. | | **Utilities** | • Lease must specify which utilities you are responsible for. | • Verify utility responsibilities at move‑in. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases require landlord approval for sublets or assignments. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Right to Repair & Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to pay for necessary repairs and deduct the cost from rent if the landlord fails to act. | • Keep receipts and document the repair process. | | **Right to Withhold Rent** | • In certain circumstances (e.g., major habitability issues), you may legally withhold rent. | • Document the issue and notify the landlord in writing. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required, having a written lease protects both parties. | • Ask for a written agreement if you’re signing a verbal lease. | ### Practical Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, receipts, emails, and a written log of any maintenance requests or landlord interactions. 2. **Know Your Notice Periods** – For month‑to‑month leases, 30 days’ notice is standard. For fixed‑term leases, check the lease for any early termination clauses. 3. **Use Certified Mail** – When sending important notices (e.g., repair requests, termination notices), use certified mail so you have proof of delivery. 4. **Seek Mediation** – If disputes arise, consider mediation services offered by local housing agencies before resorting to court. 5. **Know the Local Ordinances** – Some cities in Texas have additional tenant protections (e.g., rent control, eviction moratoria). Check your city’s ordinances. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Tenant‑rights guides, dispute resolution resources | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Fair housing complaints, discrimination resources | https://www.tchh.texas.gov/ | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | Federal fair housing information, complaint filing | https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/fair_housing_equal_opp | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Legal clinics, workshops, advocacy | Search online for “tenant rights Texas” + your city | | **Small Claims Court** | Resolve disputes over security deposits, damages | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ | Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific aspect—whether it’s how to draft a notice, what constitutes “normal wear and tear,” or how to file a discrimination complaint.
